item.title: Start Here
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Welcome — you picked a great time to start.

Pickleball is the easiest racquet sport to pick up and one of the hardest to put down. Here in Rock Hill and York County there's a friendly, fast-growing community, and you can genuinely be rallying within your first hour. Here's your no-stress path in.

Step 1 — Learn the basics (15 minutes).

It's played on a court smaller than tennis, with a paddle and a plastic ball. Games go to 11, win by 2. There's a "kitchen" (no-volley zone) at the net, and you serve underhand. That's enough to start — you'll pick up the rest by playing. Full rules FAQ →

Step 2 — Know what the numbers mean.

You'll hear people say "I'm a 3.0" or "that's a 4.0 game." Those are skill ratings from 2.5 (brand new) to 5.0+ (highly competitive). Don't worry about yours yet — most beginners are a 2.5–3.0. Skill levels explained →

Step 3 — Grab a paddle (you don't need a fancy one).

A $40–$80 beginner paddle is perfect to start. Many groups have loaner paddles too — you can play your first few times without buying anything. Beginner gear guide →

Step 4 — Show up to a beginner-friendly session.

The easiest way in is open play or a beginner clinic. See which courts are best for beginners → and find the local groups → — folks here are welcoming, and "I'm new" is the fastest way to get pulled into a game.

Step 5 — Find your people.

The community organizes through CourtReserve, Group.Me, and Facebook. We've rounded up all the links so you're not hunting. Find players & groups →

That's it. Come out, say hi, and don't worry about being new — everyone here was, once.

item.title: Skill Levels Explained
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Ever heard someone say "I'm a 3.0" or "that's a 4.0 game" and wondered what it meant? Pickleball uses skill ratings, usually from 2.5 to 5.0+, to help players find evenly-matched games. Even matches are more fun for everyone — nobody enjoys a 15–2 blowout on either side.

Here's the honest, plain-English version. Don't stress about your exact number — most people improve fast at the start, and the friendly move is to under-rate yourself and play up.

🟢 2.5 — Brand New

You're learning. You know the basic rules, can serve and return sometimes, and you're still getting a feel for the kitchen and keeping score. This is where nearly everyone starts — and it's a great place to be. Look for beginner sessions and clinics.

🟢 3.0 — Advancing Beginner

You can keep a rally going, get most serves and returns in, and you're starting to understand where to stand and hit. You're learning to "dink" (those soft shots at the net) and not just bang every ball. Consistency is the next step.

🟡 3.5 — Solid Intermediate

You sustain rallies, move to the net as a team, and mix in soft shots and drives on purpose. You know the strategy of "get to the kitchen line," and your third-shot drop is a work in progress. This is where a huge chunk of active club players live.

🟡 4.0 — Strong Intermediate

You're consistent, you place your shots, and you have a reliable third-shot drop and dinking game. You force errors, cover the court well with a partner, and rarely beat yourself. Games get tactical.

🟠 4.5 — Advanced

Few unforced errors, strong control on both soft and power shots, smart shot selection, and real teamwork. You anticipate, you attack the right balls, and you can adjust mid-game. Competitive tournament territory.

🔴 5.0+ — Highly Competitive / Pro-Level

Elite consistency, power, touch, and strategy. Rarely makes mistakes, punishes any that opponents make. Regional and national tournament players.

📊 DUPR — the modern rating

You may also hear about DUPR (Dynamic Universal Pickleball Rating), a more precise rating (roughly 2.0–8.0) based on your actual match results. Many leagues and tournaments use it. If you want one, [FILL IN: link to our club DUPR, or dupr.com]. For casual play, the 2.5–5.0 scale above is all you need.

Not sure where you land? Come to an open-play or beginner session and just play — regulars will help you find your level fast. See the friendliest spots to start in our Courts Guide →.

item.title: FAQ
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Everything a new (or curious) Rock Hill pickleball player wants to know. Can't find your answer? Contact us → — we're happy to help.

The Basics

What is pickleball?
A paddle sport that mixes tennis, ping-pong, and badminton. It's played on a court smaller than tennis, with a solid paddle and a plastic ball with holes. It's easy to learn, easy on the body, and ridiculously fun — which is why it's the fastest-growing sport in the country.

Is it hard to learn?
No — that's the magic of it. Most people are rallying within their first hour. The basics take minutes; the strategy takes a lifetime (in a good way).

What are the basic rules?
Games are usually to 11, win by 2. You serve underhand, diagonally. There's a "kitchen" (the no-volley zone) right at the net — you can't smash the ball out of the air while standing in it. The ball must bounce once on each side before players can volley. That's enough to start; you'll pick up the rest by playing. New to it all? Start with our Start Here guide →.

What's "the kitchen"?
It's the 7-foot no-volley zone on each side of the net. You can stand in it, but you can't hit the ball out of the air while you're there — you'd have to let it bounce first. It keeps the game from becoming all smashes at the net.

Getting Started

Do I need my own paddle?
Not to start. Many groups and sessions have loaner paddles, so you can try it for free first. When you're ready to buy, a $40–$80 beginner paddle is plenty. See our Gear Guide →.

What should I wear?
Comfortable athletic clothes and court shoes (tennis or dedicated court shoes — not running shoes, which don't handle the side-to-side movement well). Bring water.

Do I need to bring a partner?
Nope. Most open-play and club sessions rotate partners and opponents, so you can show up solo and play all day. Want to line someone up ahead of time? Use Find Players & Groups →.

I've never played. Where do I start?
Come to a beginner-friendly session or clinic — [FILL IN: name your best beginner spots, e.g., Shield of Faith mornings]. Read Start Here → first, then just show up. "I'm new" is the fastest way to get welcomed into a game.

Playing in Rock Hill

Where can I play in Rock Hill?
There are several options — Boyd Hill, Bleachery Fieldhouse, Shield of Faith, and Peachtree in Fort Mill. Each has its pros and cons, which we lay out honestly in the Courts Guide →.

How much does it cost to play?
It varies by location — some are free or low-cost, others charge for court time. Check each court's page in the Courts Guide → for details.

How do I reserve a court?
Most local courts use CourtReserve for bookings and open-play sign-ups. We've linked the right pages for each court in the Courts Guide → and Find Players & Groups →.

What is "open play"?
Open play is drop-in pickleball — you show up during a scheduled block, and players rotate on and off the courts. It's the easiest, most social way to get games, especially as a newcomer.

Indoor or outdoor — what's the difference?
Outdoor is weather-dependent but breezy and free-feeling; indoor (like Bleachery or Shield of Faith) means you play rain or shine and out of the summer heat. Both are great — it just depends on the day and your schedule.

How do I find people to play with?
The Rock Hill community organizes through CourtReserve, Group.Me, and Facebook. We've gathered all the links in one place — Find Players & Groups →.

Skills & Community

What do the skill numbers (2.5, 3.0, 3.5…) mean?
They're skill ratings that help match players for even, fun games. We break them all down in Skill Levels Explained →. Short version: nearly everyone starts around 2.5–3.0, and you'll improve fast.

Is pickleball good exercise?
Yes — it's a genuine workout (agility, reflexes, cardio) that's easier on the joints than running or tennis, which is part of why players of every age love it.

Can kids / seniors / total beginners play?
Absolutely — all of the above, often on the same court. It's one of the most age-friendly sports there is.

How do I get better?
Play a lot, take a clinic, and play with people slightly better than you. Check Coaches & Clinics → for local lessons.

How do I get involved with the club?
Start by joining our community links and our newsletter so you always know what's happening. [FILL IN: newsletter signup / membership link]. Then just come play — that's really all it takes.

Something on this site is out of date. Can I tell you?
Please do! We keep this resource accurate with help from players like you. Suggest an update →.

Still have a question? Contact us → — a real local player will get back to you.

item.title: About
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Built by local players who got tired of the runaround.

Getting into pickleball around Rock Hill used to mean piecing things together — a Group.Me screenshot here, a "which court is even open?" text there, and no straight answer on what any of the courts were actually like. Newcomers had it worst: a fun, welcoming sport hidden behind a wall of insider knowledge.

So we built the guide we wish we'd had.

This site isn't a booking system or a schedule — it's a resource. Honest information about every court, plain-English help for anyone new, and a directory of where the community actually lives online. Our goal is simple: make it easy for anyone in York County to find a game and fall in love with this sport.

We keep it accurate with help from players like you. Spot something outdated? Tell us.

Welcome to the community. Now go play.
